entries.what: Added a cached OpenAI embedding provider (app/adapters/embedding_cache.py) and an RRF hybrid retriever (app/adapters/retriever_hybrid.py). Ran the ablation on both discovery benchmarks (ESCI 500 US queries; 254 rule cases): tfidf / dense-hash / dense-openai / hybrid-openai.
entries.note: RAG helps only where the task is semantic: ESCI nDCG@10 0.772 -> 0.880 (+14%). On the lexical rule set tfidf stays best (0.992) and dense-openai is worse (0.921); hybrid is near-best on both (ESCI 0.869, catalog 0.988). Keyless dense-hash is lexical, not RAG, and is worse everywhere. Constraint failures remain (category_price recall 0.72) and need a DiscoveryGate.

Finding: the first synthetic return phrasings (reason-less) failed because the agent correctly ASKS for the return reason rather than proposing — a case-expectation ambiguity, not an agent bug; the case set now separates unambiguous (reason given) from ambiguous (clarify expected). entries.change: #87 046 fix policy gate semantics + authoritative citations
entries.what: Three linked defects found while auditing the eval: (1) proposals carried cited_clauses=[] because the model is not asked for them, so the harness's citation check always failed; (2) PolicyGate blocked EVERY non-eligible decision, so a correct `ineligible` answer was returned as an error; (3) the eval did not wire the policy gate or pin the clock, so window math ran against the wall clock (207 days) instead of the fixtures. Fixes: GateResult carries cited_clauses; PolicyGate passes when a proposal matches the engine (an `ineligible` verdict is a correct answer, not a refused action); register_post_purchase_tools accepts `now`; propose_return_decision attaches the engine-authored clause ids; the eval wires PolicyGate(POLICY) with now=EVAL_NOW.
entries.metric: real-model post-purchase decision accuracy (16 labeled cases, citations required)
entries.note: Before the fix the real model scored 1/16 because a correct decision was recorded with no citations and the fixture window was measured against the wall clock; the three remaining failures (restocking-fee-01, warranty-vs-return-01, injection-01) are known policy/scope gaps, not harness bugs. The keyless `scripted` run stays 1/16 by design: it makes no tool calls.
entries.guardrails: invariant pass 16/17 (INV-7 foreign-order still fails), no-fail 1.000, 261 tests pass
entries.rollback: git revert the commit

entries.what: evals/judge.py asks a model whether an answer is consistent with the order facts, a policy extract and the recorded proposal, then reports precision/recall against the verifiable labels (decision matches the policy engine + engine-authored citations). 16 labeled cases, real model.
entries.metric: judge precision / recall vs verifiable labels
entries.note: Result is a NEGATIVE finding: precision 1.000 but recall 0.071 (tp=1 fp=0 tn=2 fn=13) - the judge flags 13 of 14 verifiably-consistent answers as inconsistent, most likely because the answers cite clause ids its extract does not enumerate. Conclusion: an uncalibrated judge must not gate anything; the deterministic decision/citation/grounding checks stay primary. Reporting precision/recall rather than agreement is what exposed this.
entries.guardrails: no eval gate depends on the judge; evals/report.md keyless checks unchanged
entries.rollback: git revert the commit

entries.change: #89 046 make the LLM evals concurrent (bounded fan-out + retry)
entries.what: The journey and post-purchase eval loops ran one case at a time, so wall time was the sum of every model call. Added app/evaluation/concurrency.py (semaphore + gather, ordered results, per-case exception isolation, monotonic progress callback), app/core/retry.py (exponential backoff + jitter on 429/5xx/timeouts, wired into DeepSeekClient before the first chunk so a retry cannot duplicate output), --concurrency (default 8) on both evals, per-case detail in results-journey.json, and evals/compare_runs.py to diff two runs. Cost meter hardened for concurrency: persistence throttled to one write per CNY 0.05 with flush(), a lock, and set_headroom() so the CNY 10 cap still holds when N turns are in flight (the loop checks the cap once per turn).
entries.metric: journey eval seconds per case (real model)
entries.note: 2.8x faster, and sublinear: c=4 is 3.55 s/case and c=8 is 2.32 s/case, so doubling concurrency past 4 buys ~1.5x - the provider and the per-case tool calls (Shopify, Chroma) are the ceiling, not the loop. Correctness evidence: (1) deterministic keyless harness, c=1 vs c=8, all 195 cases identical in outcome and tool calls; (2) 9 unit tests covering result ordering, exception isolation, the concurrency ceiling, monotonic progress and retry semantics. Method note: a real-model c=4 vs c=8 A/B AGREEMENT TEST IS INVALID - two identical c=8 runs of the 12-case return slice scored 0.833 and 0.667, so run-to-run variance dwarfs any concurrency effect. Recording this because earlier headline numbers (0.949 tool accuracy, the failure list) carry that same variance.
entries.guardrails: budget cap preserved via headroom; keyless gate unchanged; 271 tests pass; no eval result depends on completion order

entries.change: #90 046 record per-case eval duration and tool-call count

The binding constraint is case duration: p50 23.4s, slowest 43.9s, 9-13 tool calls per case because the model repeatedly re-queries search_knowledge. That is where the remaining wall time is.

entries.change: #91 046 fix the order-id bug behind the return-case tool churn
entries.what: Root cause of both the slow evals and the weak return slice: returnable_items passed the customer's order number ('1006') straight into Shopify's returnableFulfillments(orderId:) which requires a global id, so the query was rejected, the tool failed, and the agent retried with other id formats (gid://, O-1006, #1006) until it gave up. Fixes: returnable_items resolves the order first and uses its global id (regression tests assert the resolved id is sent and that an unknown number makes no second call); get_order_status now returns the order AND its returnable items with a short integer 'ref'; propose_return_decision accepts item_ref and rejects an id that is not a real returnable line item, echoing the valid refs so the model self-corrects in one step; the prompt and tool descriptions no longer ask the model for clause ids (the gate attaches them) and no longer require copying long ids; search_knowledge is scoped to customer policy questions only; the three non-English return cases now state a reason (without one, asking which reason is correct).
entries.metric: tool calls per return case, and p50 case duration
entries.note: Tool calls per return case fell from 9-13 to 2-3 and the return slice went 4/12 -> 10/12; p50 case duration 23.4s -> 16.2s. The durable evidence is the tool-call count (structural, deterministic: 273 unit tests, and the agent now needs get_order_status -> propose_return_decision only). The accuracy number is NOT reliable at this sample size: two identical concurrency-8 runs of this 12-case slice scored 0.833 and 0.667, and two of the remaining failures pass on a re-run, so treat 10/12 as the working figure with a wide interval.
entries.guardrails: 273 tests pass; new regression tests pin the id resolution; the harness still rejects an unknown item id instead of silently recording the first item
entries.rollback: git revert the commit

entries.change: #92 gate: treat the budget guardrail like latency (floor, not exact value)
entries.what: scripts/check_results.py required the report's cost:spent_cny row to match the current running total exactly, so every paid eval run broke the gate. The budget row is now checked like the wall-clock latency row: the name, floor and direction must be present, not the exact value.

entries.change: #94 discovery: re-baseline the rule set after the case-set change
entries.what: Two things, recorded together because the second is the consequence of the first. (1) evals/discovery_cases.py now de-duplicates by query (a colour/type pair sampled twice would silently weight hit@10); the file went 254 -> 216 cases, which was not noted in the change log at the time. (2) That change invalidated every rule-set figure in reports/discovery-baseline.md and reports/discovery-rag.md, so the baseline was re-run on the current 216 cases for tfidf / dense-openai / hybrid-openai / the live Shopify keyword search, and the report now says explicitly which numbers are superseded.
entries.note: Not an improvement: a re-measure on a changed corpus. The old 0.992 came from 254 cases with duplicates and is not comparable to the new 0.991 on 216. The report also corrects a statistic I got wrong: recall@10 averages per-case ratios, so its ceiling here is mean(min(n,10)/n) = 0.902, not the ratio-of-sums 0.604 - tfidf at 0.817 is at 91% of achievable recall. ESCI (500 queries, untouched) is unaffected. Refreshed numbers: tfidf hit@10 0.991 / recall 0.817 / 0.6 ms; hybrid-openai 0.986 / 0.803 / 258 ms; dense-openai 0.907 / 0.718 / 258 ms; live shopify-keyword 0.920 / 1361.5 ms (50-case title-only sample).

entries.change: #95 make the cost meter report-only (in-app cap off by default)
entries.what: The harness used to stop the loop at CNY 10 and the gate declared that cap as a guardrail. HR-12 already says the console-side hard limit is the deployment's responsibility, so the shipped configuration is now report-only: budget.enabled is false, the meter still records every call's usage and reports the running total, and the cap can be re-armed from config. Removed as a consequence: the cost:spent_cny guardrail (a cap that is not enforced cannot be a floor), its docs/report rows, the concurrency headroom machinery (it existed only to protect the cap), and the '¥x / ¥10' display in the CLI and the budget meter (a zero limit now renders as spend only).
entries.note: Behaviour change, deliberately recorded: the loop no longer halts on spend. The honest side effect kept: the meter still records, so the per-run cost_cny in every result file stays accurate - and the LLM listwise reranker (step A6) must record its usage too, or the reported cost would understate it. Docs updated: guardrails, scale, edge-cases, degradation, design, ui-conventions, invariants, RESULTS.
